title: Oral Presentation Skills
subtitle: Narrativ versjon
description: A practical guide to speaking with confidence -- structuring a presentation, designing slides that support rather than replace you, and handling tough questions in the Q&A.
competenceGoals: give well-structured oral presentations on complex topics and adapt the language to the purpose and audience
use rhetorical devices and presentation techniques to engage an audience

content.content:
## Speaking with Confidence and Purpose

The ability to present ideas clearly and persuasively to an audience is one of the most valuable skills you can develop -- in school, in the workplace, and in life. Whether you are presenting a project in class, pitching an idea at work, or speaking at a community event, effective presentation skills make the difference between being heard and being ignored.

Many students dread oral presentations. The good news is that presentation skills can be learned and improved with practice. The most compelling speakers are not born with a special gift -- they have developed their skills through preparation, practice, and reflection. In this chapter you will learn to structure a presentation using the three-part model, apply techniques for engaging an audience, design effective visual aids, manage nervousness, and handle questions professionally. Nervousness is normal and manageable; thorough preparation is your best tool.

## Structure and Delivery

Every effective presentation follows a clear three-part structure: introduction, body, and conclusion. The **introduction** (10-15% of total time) should grab attention, establish credibility, and preview the talk. It needs a **hook** -- a surprising statistic ("Did you know the average person spends 7 hours a day looking at a screen?"), a thought-provoking question, a brief anecdote, or a bold statement -- followed by a clear topic statement, a note on relevance, and a roadmap of the main points. The **body** (75-80% of time) presents your main arguments. Limit yourself to **3-4 main points** (audiences struggle to retain more), use clear signposting ("My first point is...," "Moving on to my second argument..."), support each point with evidence, and use transitions to maintain flow. The **conclusion** (10-15%) should signal the ending, summarize the main points, restate the core message, and end memorably -- never with "That's it" or "I'm done," but with a call to action, a powerful quote, or a return to the opening hook.

Content is only half the equation -- *how* you deliver it matters just as much. In **voice and speech**, vary your pace (around 130-150 words per minute), project your volume, use strategic pauses to let key points sink in, avoid monotone, and articulate clearly. In **body language**, make eye contact with different sections of the audience (holding it 2-3 seconds at a time), stand straight but relaxed, use natural gestures, move purposefully rather than pacing randomly, and match your facial expressions to your content. To engage the audience, ask questions ("How many of you have...?"), use humour sparingly, tell stories, apply the "rule of three" (grouping ideas in threes), and include interactive elements like quick polls. A strong opening hook for a talk on fast fashion, for example, might be: "Every second, the equivalent of one garbage truck of textiles is landfilled or burned" -- a statistic that grips the audience in under a minute.

exercise.task: Test yourself on structure and delivery:

questions.task: How many main points should a presentation body typically have?

options.text: 3-4 main points, since audiences struggle to retain more

questions.solution: Limit the body to 3-4 main points, because audiences struggle to retain more. Use clear signposting and support each point with evidence.

questions.task: What should the introduction of a presentation include?

options.text: A hook, a topic statement, a note on relevance, and a roadmap

questions.solution: The introduction (10-15% of time) should grab attention with a hook, state the topic, explain its relevance, and preview the main points with a roadmap.

questions.task: What is a recommended speaking pace for a presentation?

options.text: As fast as possible to save time
Around 130-150 words per minute, with variation for emphasis

questions.solution: Aim for about 130-150 words per minute, varying your pace -- slowing down for key points -- and using strategic pauses. Avoid monotone delivery.

questions.task: How should you end a presentation?

options.text: Memorably -- with a call to action, a quote, or a return to the opening hook

questions.solution: End memorably with a call to action, a powerful quote, or a return to the opening hook -- never with a flat 'That's it' or 'I'm done.'

content.content:
## Visual Aids and Handling Questions

Visual aids -- slides, images, videos, props -- should **support** your message, not replace it. The audience should be listening to *you*, not reading your slides. A useful guideline is the **6-by-6 rule**: no more than 6 bullet points per slide, and no more than 6 words per bullet point. Best practices include one idea per slide, high-quality images (a powerful image communicates more than a wall of text), minimal text (keywords, not full sentences), consistent design, readable fonts (minimum 24pt, sans-serif), high contrast, and data visualization (graphs instead of tables of numbers). Common mistakes to avoid: reading directly from your slides (the audience reads faster than you speak), distracting animations, cramming too much on one slide, and having more slides than minutes in your presentation.

The Q&A session is where many presenters falter, but it can be managed with skill. A **weak response** is dismissive and defensive: "No, that's not true. Wind energy is great and critics just support fossil fuels." A **strong response** acknowledges the concern and answers with evidence: "Thank you for raising that point... You're right that wind turbines do pose risks to bird populations, and this is an area of ongoing research. Studies by the Audubon Society have found that proper placement... can significantly reduce bird mortality. As for cost, while the initial investment is substantial, operational costs have decreased by over 70% in the past decade..." The effective Q&A strategies are to listen to the full question before responding, repeat or rephrase it so everyone can hear, acknowledge the validity of the concern (this builds credibility), respond with evidence rather than opinion, admit honestly when you do not know ("That's a great question -- I don't have the exact data, but I'd be happy to follow up"), stay calm even if the question is hostile, and keep answers concise (30-60 seconds). Above all, remember that a great presentation is a conversation with your audience, not a performance for them.

exercise.task: Test yourself on visual aids and Q&A:

questions.task: What is the '6-by-6 rule' for slides?

options.text: No more than 6 bullet points per slide and 6 words per bullet point

questions.solution: The 6-by-6 rule recommends no more than 6 bullet points per slide and no more than 6 words per bullet point. If you need more text, use more slides.

questions.task: What is a common mistake with presentation slides?

options.text: Reading directly from the slides, since the audience can read faster than you speak

questions.solution: Reading directly from slides is a common mistake -- the audience reads faster than you speak. Slides should support you with keywords and images, not replace your speech.

questions.task: What is the best way to handle a critical question in Q&A?

options.text: Dismiss it as wrong and get defensive
Acknowledge the concern's validity and respond with evidence, staying calm

questions.solution: A strong Q&A response acknowledges the concern's validity (which builds credibility), responds with evidence rather than opinion, and stays calm even if the question is hostile.

questions.task: What should you do if you do not know the answer to a question?

options.text: Pretend you did not hear the question
Admit it honestly and offer to follow up

questions.solution: It is best to admit honestly when you don't know -- 'That's a great question; I don't have the exact data, but I'd be happy to follow up' -- rather than inventing an answer.

content.content:
## Summary

Effective oral presentations rest on structure, delivery, visual aids, and Q&A skill. Every presentation needs a clear **introduction** (with a hook), **body** (3-4 main points), and **conclusion** (with a memorable ending). **Delivery** is as important as content -- voice variation, eye contact, purposeful movement, and strategic pauses make the difference between forgettable and memorable. **Visual aids** should support, not replace, the speaker: follow the 6-by-6 rule, use high-quality images, and never read directly from slides. **Q&A sessions** require active listening, acknowledgment of the questioner, evidence-based responses, and the honesty to say "I don't know" when appropriate. Nervousness is normal and manageable through preparation. The most important principle: a great presentation is a conversation with your audience, not a performance for them.
